newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco's economy to picks up after contracting.
newsitem.headline: Morocco's economy to picks up after contracting.

text.p: Morocco's economy has gathered steam after a slow start, with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecast to rise by more than 10 percent this year after a catastrophic drought sent it plunging by 7.6 percent in 1995.

"I am optimistic because the results are favourable. There is a net improvement in the balances. And the ratios, as you can see from the figures, are positive," Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj told Reuters on Friday.
Kabbaj, confirming figures given to the cabinet on Thursday and carried on the official news agency MAP, said in reference to GDP: "We hope to go over 10 percent growth this year."

He had told the cabinet the economy was characterised by "positive financial indicators" such as an increase of global monetary reserves to three billion dirhams ($344.8 million) at the end of July 1996.

According to the figures, public savings were up to 5.7 billion dirhams, a rise of 2.6 billion compared with end of August 1995, while revenue from company taxes was up by about 45 percent and income tax revenue was up by more than 10 percent.

Kabbaj also told the cabinet that after stagnation in the first half of the year, total credits of 3.6 billion dirhams had been granted in July. These, with loans from state banks, were mainly for farming and construction, including the hotel sector.
"Bank deposits recorded an important increase, reaching 3.7 billion dirhams in July after a fall during the first six months of this year," he said.
Kabbaj earlier this month had dismissed rumours of a possible devaluation of the dirham, saying "we have no plans to devalue our national currency".
All economic indicators showed "the resumption of economic activity", he said, including the main indicators on the Casablanca bourse.
Forty-six companies are listed on the bourse, whose traded volume on Thursday totalled 48.5 million dirhams.

The Casablanca stock market has seen increasing activity as Rabat's privatisation plans have gone ahead, with 114 state enterprises slated to be sold off by the end of 1998 when the programme was launched in 1993. So far, more than 40 firms have been sold.

Earlier this month, the country's ONA Group bought controlling stakes in four mines for the equivalent of $75 million. Next month, the state plans to float 30 percent of the FERTIMA feriliser firm on the bourse at 120 million dirhams ($13.7 million).
But there are shadows hanging over future exports to the European Union, which took three-quarters of Morocco's important citrus fruit exports in 1995.

Farmers in this North African country of 27 million people have been angered by an EU decision they said last week would cut their exports of citrus and tomatoes and expose them to unfair competition from EU members like Spain.
Agriculture and food products in the first five months of this year, the latest figures from the official Office des Changes, made up 37 percent of Morocco's total exports.
This was dominated by citrus fruit exports valued at 1.309 billion dirhams, compared with 838 million in the first five months of 1995. ($1 = 8.7 dirhams)
